600.bp: When you want product recommendations, you want them fast—not waiting for a complex pipeline to check dozens of factors. Generative recommendation is a direct approach: given your history, a language model just outputs items one by one, like writing a sequence. The appeal is speed and efficiency: no intermediate ranking step, no separate scoring systems.
600.wh: The trap is what happens as the model predicts each item: early predictions build on the user's history, but later predictions must lean on earlier outputs. If the first item skews toward one type (say, electronics), every step after inherits that bias and tends to pick more electronics. The model keeps amplifying its own mistakes, and users get stuck in a narrow set of recommendations.
600.ap: The paper proposes CARE: instead of locking in the user history once at the start, they feed progressively finer details about what the user clicked as they generate each item. They also run multiple reasoning steps in parallel for each new item, asking 'given what we know so far, what should come next?' in multiple ways, then pick the best. This splits the thinking load across more computation, which counters the buildup of bias.
600.ww: The reason this works is simple: if you're making a guess, looking at more angles before guessing reduces the chance you'll repeat your last mistake. More detailed history means you're not relying on a compressed, biased summary. Parallel reasoning lets the model escape its own groove by considering fresh viewpoints on the same history.
600.po: The outcome is more diverse recommendations—when you ask for suggestions, you get actual variety instead of 50 variants of the same thing. This makes the tool more useful, and users stay longer because browsing feels fresh.

601.bp: Hate speech and violent content spread on platforms like YouTube and TikTok at scale. Automated systems need to catch and flag these videos, but they also need to explain what they saw—otherwise, creators can't defend themselves, and platforms can't justify removals to regulators who demand transparency.
601.wh: Most systems blend video, sound, and text into one fuzzy representation and guess whether it's hateful. This black-box approach is fast but gives no evidence: you can't point to the frame or phrase and say 'this is the problem.' Meanwhile, real hate videos use tricks—one audio stream is innocent, the text is coded, the visuals are subtle—so you can miss it by looking at only one signal.
601.ap: This paper treats each signal—what's shown, what's said, what's written, and context—as independent pieces of evidence. They extract objects in frames, transcribed speech, text from subtitles, and look up relevant background info. Each gets scored on how much it contributes to a hate verdict, and the system notes when signals agree, conflict, or are missing. A fallback rule-based baseline handles obvious cases; an optional LLM digs into ambiguous ones.
601.ww: The power is in separation: by keeping signals apart, you can see which ones actually matter for the decision. If a video is flagged, you can point to three specific things (that face, that phrase, that historical context), not just 'the model said so.' Conflicts between signals—audio says one thing, visuals another—are now visible clues that the creator might be being deceptive.
601.po: Creators and regulators can audit these decisions. If a video is removed, the system explains why with concrete evidence. This builds trust even when people disagree with the judgment, because the reasoning is laid bare.

602.bp: Smartphone automation—asking an AI to tap buttons, fill forms, and navigate apps—is useful for accessibility and task automation. But even the best agents fail on complex tasks because they don't know how apps work. They might know 'tap the blue button' but not which field to fill or why an error occurred.
602.wh: The obvious fix is to give the agent a manual for every app—but there are millions of apps, and manuals are static while apps change. An agent also has gaps: it understands buttons but not the intent behind a flow, or gets confused on the third step of a five-step task because it forgot the goal.
602.ap: The paper proposes a curiosity mechanism: as the agent works, it measures uncertainty—when it's unsure about the next step, it signals 'I need help.' At that moment, the system retrieves relevant app documentation, code examples, or past successful task logs, and packages them into structured 'AppCards' that encode what each button does, what parameters it accepts, and common patterns. The agent reads the AppCard and continues, using the new knowledge.
602.ww: The magic is timing: you don't hand the agent a library upfront—you give it just what it needs when confusion strikes. This is like a human looking up a recipe only when stuck on the next step. It keeps the agent's focus narrow and prevents information overload, while the curated examples show what success looks like.
602.po: The agent's success rate on complex tasks jumps from ~82% to ~89%. Multi-step tasks—like booking a hotel and then opening email—nearly double in success because the agent can connect steps via AppCard patterns. The system becomes reliable enough for real users.

603.bp: Predicting major geopolitical events weeks in advance could help policymakers prepare, traders hedge, and emergency responders ready resources. The raw material is news articles, social media posts, and analysis buried in the internet—the signal is there, but extracting it is hard.
603.wh: Language models can read and reason, but when you ask them to predict from a pile of news, they make two mistakes. First, they miss buried clues: the causal chain (A led to B which led to C) or subtle patterns (when tension rises, conflict follows in a specific timeframe). Second, they 'hallucinate'—invent plausible-sounding details that sound right but are wrong, corrupting the forecast.
603.ap: BRSC reasons in two directions at once. One path is temporal: it maps historical events on a timeline, spots trends, and extrapolates forward—like seeing 'tensions have risen for three weeks, conflict likelihood is rising.' The other path is synchronic: within a given week, it digs for hidden connections between events and entities, building a richer understanding of what might happen next. When the LLM makes claims, a self-correction step asks 'does this match what the text actually says?' and fixes hallucinations.
603.ww: Looking backward (timeline trends) and sideways (current connections) gives two independent views of the same question. If both point to conflict, confidence rises. If they disagree, the system flags uncertainty rather than guessing. Asking the model to check itself—'is this real or invented?'—catches the most egregious hallucinations.
603.po: The model predicts international events more accurately, catching real risks rather than false alarms. In field tests on relations between nations, BRSC beats baselines, reducing the noise that derails real prediction systems.

604.bp: Robots and drones that understand images and follow instructions are proliferating—in warehouses, farms, and rescue operations. But these vision-language-action models are deployed from public repositories, exposing a supply chain risk: an adversary with access to the server could subtly alter the model to make robots misbehave in dangerous ways.
604.wh: A direct attack like flipping pixels is too obvious: the robot or a monitor would catch severe distortion and stop. But if you nudge only certain pixels—maybe the edges of an obstacle, or part of a tool—the image still looks normal to humans while the model's internal reasoning breaks. The challenge is breaking the link between 'I see object X' and 'I should do action Y' without raising alarms.
604.ap: MAVLA injects tiny perturbations into specific regions of images—parts that matter for understanding the scene or following the instruction. It balances two goals: break the model's ability to align what it sees with what it's asked to do (by maximizing 'disagreement' between vision and language pathways), while keeping the visual change imperceptible to humans. Four loss functions work together to maximize misalignment while preserving visual stealth.
604.ww: The reason this works is that neural networks rely on patterns spread throughout the image. By perturbing task-relevant regions—the edges of a box, part of a hand gesture—you corrupt the features the model uses for reasoning without changing what a human sees. The model still 'sees' the image, but it interprets it wrongly.
604.po: At 40% perturbation (modest changes), robot task success drops by 70%. A robot told 'pick up the red cup' might reach for the table instead. Worse, the attack looks innocent under visual inspection. The paper serves as a red-team test: it shows that VLA models need defenses, and hints at what those defenses should protect against.

605.bp: Self-driving vehicles connected to satellites can cover remote areas, but they face hacking threats across multiple channels: the vehicle's internal bus (CAN), messages from other vehicles (V2X), and sensors. A cloud-based defense system is too slow—500-600ms latency means the vehicle crashes before a server responds. Protection must happen on-board, instantly.
605.wh: The naive approach is to monitor each threat stream separately: flag anomalies in the CAN bus, separately flag anomalies in sensor data, separately flag anomalies in V2X. But an adversary can coordinate: send a plausible CAN message that contradicts a sensor reading in a way that each detector sees as slightly off but not flagged. Multi-channel attacks need multi-channel defenses.
605.ap: MARIS-ADS collects 41 CAN signals, 37 V2X signals, and 28 sensor streams, then uses attention—a mechanism that weights which signals matter most—to fuse them. It ranks signals by how much they contribute to the anomaly score, and drops the least relevant ones (83% reduction in data). Then it applies physics constraints: is the claimed vehicle state physically possible? Did the message violate V2X protocol? Invalid claims are blocked outright.
605.ww: The insight is that anomalies across channels leave a fingerprint. Real sensor conflicts (a camera sees an obstacle the radar doesn't) have explanations; attack-generated conflicts often violate the laws of physics or protocol rules. By fusing data and checking physical feasibility, you catch coordinated attacks that fool single-channel detectors.
605.po: The system rejects 97% of attacks that hit multiple channels at once, versus 12-34% from systems watching one channel. Real-world inference takes 0.31 milliseconds—fast enough for safety-critical braking. The vehicle can decide whether to stop or swerve before it travels another meter.

606.bp: Web applications—banking sites, e-commerce platforms, SaaS dashboards—have security holes that hackers exploit. Finding them before deployment is critical. But web apps are complex, and security testing tools often miss vulnerabilities because the input space is huge (millions of possible form submissions).
606.wh: Closed-box fuzzing means you can't see the application's internals; you only have network responses. Without that visibility, testers blindly hammer the app with random inputs. Most waste effort on unreachable code or harmless behaviors. Attackers also hide vulnerabilities with defensive logic: trigger a SQL injection only under specific conditions, so random testing misses it.
606.ap: Zelda infers hints from the web responses themselves. When a response contains new text, an error message, or different timing, that's feedback that something changed—the input affected the app. Zelda learns these patterns and focuses on inputs that produce novel responses. It then uses two strategies: broad exploration to cover different code paths, and targeted exploitation to chain inputs together to trigger deep flaws (like the SQL injection that only manifests after five clicks).
606.ww: The reasoning is that every response is a signal. An error page means 'you found an edge case'; a slow response means 'this input triggered complex logic.' By treating responses as feedback, Zelda does directed testing instead of random guessing. Combining exploration (map the app) with exploitation (dig into interesting behaviors) lets it balance breadth and depth.
606.po: Zelda found 182 vulnerabilities in 15 real web apps, outperforming six other tools. In the wild, it discovered 29 unknown vulnerabilities that earned CVEs. Developers can now find and patch real risks before deployment.

607.bp: When a user scrolls through an e-commerce feed, the platform wants to maximize multiple goals: get them to buy something, keep them engaged with more views, and keep them scrolling (not closing the app). These sound aligned, but they conflict: a high-conversion item might bore them into leaving, while an engaging item might go unwatched.
607.wh: The typical ranking system optimizes one goal at a time, then combines scores. But in e-commerce, especially with immersive swiping, behaviors are intertwined: clicking an item is often followed by viewing more items is often followed by buying. Optimizing one pushes against the others. Also, the full-screen UI creates 'temporal greedy traps': the system picks the best item for the current screen, but that choice locks out the ideal item for the next screen.
607.ap: STCRank uses spatial collaboration: within each screen, it manages multi-objective trade-offs by modeling which objectives conflict (when one rises, another falls) and steering toward a balanced frontier of solutions instead of maximizing each separately. Temporal collaboration: it looks ahead to the next screens and considers how today's choice limits tomorrow's options, reducing greedy mistakes. The system treats each screen as a step in a longer sequence.
607.ww: The insight is that objectives in sequential recommendation aren't independent—they're coupled through user behavior and UI design. By explicitly modeling their conflicts and temporal dependencies, the system avoids the trap of local optimization at each screen. It's like planning a meal: appetizer choice affects how good the main course feels.
607.po: The ranking system balances goals better: users see items they want to click, items worth viewing, and are motivated to keep scrolling. Engagement and conversion both rise—no longer at odds. On a platform with millions of daily users, this shift in balance drives measurable value.

608.bp: When hospitals or devices can't share raw data (due to privacy), they can still benefit from machine learning through federated learning: each site trains a model locally, and they share learned patterns—not data. The challenge is when sites have different patient types: a rural clinic's data distribution differs from an urban hospital's.
608.wh: Existing federated learning treats each class (disease type) as one holistic pattern and shares that pattern across sites. But a single pattern is too rigid: one site might see 'cardiac disease' as mostly hypertension, another as mostly arrhythmia. A rigid class pattern doesn't adapt. Also, if you have 1000 disease classes, sharing 1000 patterns wastes communication.
608.ap: FedVPL decomposes each class into semantic building blocks—'visual primitives' like 'inflammation pattern', 'structural change', 'severity marker'—then shares those reusable pieces. A rural clinic can mix primitives differently than an urban hospital, personalizing the model. It uses a language model to align primitives semantically (ensuring 'inflammation' means the same thing everywhere) without transmitting model parameters, saving communication.
608.ww: The power is modularity: instead of 'cardiac disease', you share 'the inflammation look' and 'the electrical disturbance pattern.' Sites reuse and recombine, tailoring to local data without relearning everything from scratch. Language models provide a common semantic bridge so 'inflammation' means the same thing at every site.
608.po: Models generalize better across sites because they're built from sharable, reusable pieces. Communication overhead drops (doesn't scale with the number of classes), and each site still personalizes to its patient population. Federated learning becomes practical for real healthcare networks.

609.bp: Graph neural networks power recommendation systems, fraud detection, and knowledge graphs. But in the real world, these graphs evolve: new entities appear, relationships change, the distribution of data shifts. Retraining the model from scratch each time is expensive. The goal is to adapt the model to new data without forgetting old patterns.
609.wh: Continual learning in graphs is tricky because you can't simply fine-tune—that destroys what the model learned before (catastrophic forgetting). Standard fixes like replaying old data are expensive: you'd need to store and replay millions of old edges. The trap is that a model adapted to the new domain forgets the old one.
609.ap: STEM uses a state-space controller that evolves continuously. Imagine the 'state' of the domain—what the graphs look like—as a hidden variable that changes over time. As new graph data arrives, STEM updates this state, then uses it to generate lightweight adapters that modify the frozen base model. Unlike linear state-space models, STEM allows the state transitions to be nonlinear and depend on the input, capturing the true dynamics of domain evolution. A penalty on adapter changes prevents wild swings that destroy past knowledge.
609.ww: The insight is that you don't need to retrain or replay data; you need to track how the domain is shifting and adapt smoothly. By modeling the domain's state and generating parameterized adaptations, the system adjusts to new data while regularizing the changes to maintain stability. It's like adjusting a compass needle gradually rather than spinning it.
609.po: The model adapts to new graphs while remembering old patterns. No memory replay, minimal overhead, and theoretical guarantees that forgetting is mitigated. Continual learning becomes practical for production systems where graphs and distributions never stop changing.

610.bp: Knowing where a social media user lives is useful for advertisers, researchers, and emergency responders. But users rarely post their location, and when data is scarce, the model struggles. The challenge is to infer location from sparse posts, bios, and profile information using limited labeled examples.
610.wh: Social media profiles are heterogeneous: one user's location signal might be a check-in, another's might be a mention of a local landmark, another's might be implicit (their language or cultural references). Standard methods struggle when there are few labeled examples and signals are noisy or conflicting.
610.ap: FewUser uses two components: first, contrastive learning—a technique that teaches the model to pull similar users close and push different ones apart, learning robust user representations from few examples. Second, it uses prompting: templated questions that adapt a pre-trained language model to the geolocation task, linking user text and location knowledge through 'hard' prompts (specific locations), 'soft' prompts (learned patterns), and 'semi-soft' prompts (hybrid). Hard negative mining ensures the model learns to distinguish tricky cases.
610.ww: The reason this works with few examples is that the pre-trained language model already knows geography and language—you just need to connect that knowledge to the user. Contrastive learning lets the model learn from unlabeled data too. Mixing hard, soft, and semi-soft prompts bridges the gap between generic language knowledge and specific user clues.
610.po: The model infers where users live more accurately, even with few labeled examples. On new datasets (TwiU and FliU) and public benchmarks, FewUser consistently outperforms baselines. Researchers and platforms can now estimate location for privacy-sensitive tasks without labeled data.

611.bp: When a recommender suggests a movie, you want to know why: 'because you liked this other film,' or 'because others who liked your taste enjoyed it.' Explainable recommendation builds trust. But explanations must be personalized and sensible, not generic boilerplate.
611.wh: Generating good explanations is hard because the model must choose which pieces of a user's history to highlight and construct a plausible narrative. If history is sparse, explanations become repetitive. If you fuse text (item reviews, descriptions) and collaborative signals (ratings from similar users) naively, they can conflict: the text says this is a thriller, but collaborative patterns say comedies match this user better.
611.ap: This paper systematically tests how to blend textual and collaborative signals in a sequence-aware model. It explores: pooling strategies (how to aggregate many reviews into one summary), fusion mechanisms (when and how to combine text and numbers—early, late, or via Transformer), and training regimes. The goal is to find the recipe that generates explanations which are both accurate and helpful.
611.ww: The mechanistic insight is that text and collaborative signals capture different truths: text describes what an item is, collaborative data describes who will like it. Fusing them at the right stage (and in the right way) lets explanations cite both 'the plot matches your taste' and 'users like you rated it highly'—richer reasoning than either alone.
611.po: When the model finds the right recipe, recommendations improve and explanations become more coherent and useful. Users see the reasoning ('you watched three thrillers, and this one has similar pacing') rather than arbitrary suggestions. Trust increases, and recommendations feel personalized.

612.bp: Large language models can reason over user behavior and predict what to recommend next. But users have massive click histories—millions of sessions—and LLMs have limited context windows. Also, LLMs sometimes invent preferences that don't exist ('this user wants kitchen appliances' when they only clicked once by accident). The model must balance a huge behavior history with reliable preference inference.
612.wh: You can't just feed all user clicks to an LLM—the context window overflows. You could sample clicks, but that loses information. You could summarize, but LLMs tend to amplify whichever preference they mentioned first, creating hallucinated persistence. An LLM might invent 'this user loves jazz' because the first song played was jazz, then stick to it despite contradictory behavior.
612.ap: Rec2 segments the user's behavior into chunks, then builds preferences one chunk at a time. For each chunk, the LLM infers what the user wanted, and the next chunk's behavior is treated as feedback: 'did my inference match what they actually did?' This reinforcement signal corrects hallucinations. After processing all chunks, a dynamic learning module captures how preferences evolve over time and fuses them into a single, long-term preference representation.
612.ww: The insight is to use the future as a teacher: if your inference about 'chunk 1' was wrong, the user's actions in 'chunk 2' will contradict it. By penalizing inferences that don't predict the next behavior, you suppress hallucinations. Segmentation lets you handle long histories without overwhelming the context window, and the reinforcement signal keeps the LLM honest.
612.po: The model makes more reliable recommendations because it infers real user preferences, not invented ones. Even on long histories with diverse behaviors, the system captures genuine intent. Recommendation quality improves, and the model avoids the pitfall of LLM hallucinations—a common failure mode in real systems.

613.bp: Knowledge graphs—structured databases of facts and relationships—grow constantly as new discoveries emerge and new entities are added. The embeddings that power searches and link prediction must update without forgetting: if a graph gains 1000 new drugs, the model must learn their embeddings and remain accurate on the existing 10,000.
613.wh: Most embedding libraries are designed for static graphs and provide no continual learning mechanism. Retraining from scratch is expensive. Naive fine-tuning forgets old embeddings (catastrophic forgetting). Existing continual KGE methods are fragmented—each paper uses a different framework—making them hard to use and compare in practice.
613.ap: This paper extends PyKEEN, a popular embedding library, to handle continual updates. When new entities arrive, it initializes their embeddings smartly—using information from related entities rather than random vectors. It adds metrics that measure both accuracy on new facts and forgetting on old ones, and provides a training interface with dashboards to track embedding evolution over time.
613.ww: The advantage is infrastructure: by embedding continual learning into an existing, widely-used library, researchers and practitioners can experiment and deploy without building from scratch. Smart initialization means new entities aren't completely blind; tracking forgetting alongside accuracy keeps the metric honest about trade-offs.
613.po: Knowledge graphs can be maintained as living systems: new facts are learned, old facts remain accurate, and the tools to experiment and audit this process are available to everyone. This enables production systems where graphs and their embeddings evolve together.

614.bp: Teaching students to code requires understanding what they know—which concepts they grasp and which trip them up. A knowledge tracing system models this and predicts whether a student will solve the next problem. For programming, this is harder than traditional subjects because success depends on logical reasoning, not just concept knowledge, and the feedback is noisy.
614.wh: Standard knowledge tracing models assume binary correctness (right or wrong) and focus on concept knowledge. But coding problems often give partial credit (pass 7 of 10 test cases, so 70% correct), which is noisy feedback. A student's logic might be sound but inefficient, failing one test case. The model misses this nuance and focuses only on whether concepts are known.
614.ap: MLPKT uses a language model to enrich feedback: it analyzes each failed submission, identifies the root cause (logic error, off-by-one, timeout), and assigns a meaningful label instead of just 'wrong.' It then models student knowledge across three levels: concept (does the student know recursion?), logical reasoning (can they trace a complex flow?), and problem-specific understanding (can they adapt to this specific task?). A three-phase training process refines knowledge estimates at each level.
614.ww: The insight is that programming fails for rich reasons, and the model must understand them to predict future success. By tracing why code fails (via an LLM) and building multi-dimensional knowledge models, the system captures the true state of a student's abilities. Partial scores and noisy feedback become interpretable signals, not noise.
614.po: The model predicts student performance on future problems more accurately, allowing tutoring systems to target instruction where it matters. A student who understands concepts but lacks logical reasoning gets different help than one who struggles with language syntax. Personalized learning becomes possible at scale.
